zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The supplied page subset was consulted after independent scan reading for lexical and coverage comparison. Corrections and English comments are reviewer-authored; this copy's printed forms are determined from its scan.

runs.text: pouco encolhidas com que os falcões arremetem

lines.note: Continues f372's description of a hawk's wings, somewhat drawn in for its attack. Enlargement supports pouco, encolhidas, and arremetem; falcões has its tilde over o, without the OCR's extra nasal a.
The wings allow the hawk to strike with greater force. Taka no noshiba wo tsukoo begins an example of using this manner of flight; tçu- continues below.

runs.text: Vſar o falcão desta maneira de voo pera

lines.note: Completes tçucǒ, the verb for using the wing action. The Portuguese explicitly reads voo, with two o letters, rather than OCR vo, and continues with the purpose of attacking.
Arremeter supplies the purpose of the hawk's wing movement: to attack or strike. This closes the entry continued from f372.

runs.text: O telhar de taboas muito acumula-

lines.note: Noshibuki denotes roofing with closely overlapping boards. The scan separates muito acumula-; the OCR's extra r and final point do not reproduce the visible word division and hyphen.

runs.text: das hũas ſobre as outras, & pregadas.

lines.note: Completes acumuladas and says the boards overlap one another and are nailed in place. The description concerns the roof's construction, not a separate material name.
Noshibuki ni suru means roofing in this manner. The Japanese example directly refers back to the overlapping, nailed boards.
No yama denotes fields and mountains. The printed space between No and yama is retained rather than joining the expression into a modern compound.
Noyaki denotes burning fields. Noya- begins the same noun with its object particle in the example on the next row.
Completes noyaki wo suru, carrying out field burning. This Japanese-only continuation is an example, not a new headword.
Noye fushi describes vegetation bending or moving with the wind. The printed two-word headword and the abbreviated ſu ending are retained; cõfor- continues the Portuguese conforme.
Completes conforme ao vento. Kusa ga kaze ni noye begins the example of grass bending before the wind; caje is the dictionary's spelling of kaze.
Fusu completes noye fusu; nabiku is supplied as a Japanese synonym. Idẽ confirms the same meaning, then per begins the figurative-use marker continued below.
The figurative sense is yielding and submitting. It extends the grass bending before the wind to a person's submission rather than introducing an unrelated verb.
Noozoo is explained as making well, yoo tsukuru, or a well-made work. The scan has no full stop after obra; that noun continues into its modifier on the next row.
Completes obra bem feita and gives noozoo no shu, the person who makes something well. The nasal abbreviation bẽ is retained and its object follows below.

runs.text: algũa obra de mãos, i, bom official.

lines.note: The person makes some manual work well and is therefore a good craftsman. The printed i is explanatory, and mãos retains its tilde over a.

runs.text: Couſa pera deſejar, ou que ſe de-

lines.note: Nozomashii means desirable or something desired. The scan reads deſejar without the OCR's extra i, and the final de- visibly divides the following Portuguese verb.
Completes de-ſeja, 'is desired'. This short Portuguese continuation belongs to the adjective nozomashii.
Gives the corresponding -sa noun and long-u adverbial form of nozomashii. Both forms occupy one physical row; the caron in Nozomaxǔ is preserved.
Nozomi first means desiring or wanting. The printed circumflex in ôda is retained as principal-part notation; the following examples develop the approaching or facing sense.
Toki ni nozomu is explained as the hour approaching. This use concerns reaching an occasion, not simply desiring time.
Saigo ni nozomu is being at the point of death. The Portuguese states imminence, matching the approach to one's end.
Senjoo ni nozomu is presented as approaching battle. The Portuguese begins 'the time approaches' and names battle on the next row; the caron in Xengiǒni is visible.
Completes 'the time of battle'. The scan reads da batalha, correcting both the preposition and the OCR's malformed tataha.
The noun nozomi means desire. Nozomi wo tassuru illustrates bringing a wish to fulfilment, with an alternative verb on the next row.
Toguru is the alternative for fulfilling the desire. Comprir is the printed historical spelling; Nozo- begins another example containing the same noun.
Completes nozomi wo okosu and offers nozomi ni zonzuru as an alternative expression for desiring or developing a wish. The printed positional v in vocoſu is not replaced with modern o.
Completes Deſejar and adds the sense of desire arising. This closes the noun's examples before the unrelated peeping verb.
Nozoki means peeping or looking covertly. The example starts a fear-concessive phrase; no comma is visible after Vt in this occurrence, unlike the clear comma earlier in the column.
Completes vosoroxi nagara nozoite mireba, looking despite being afraid. The printed xi ending and nozoite are preserved rather than expanded to modern forms.

runs.text: couſa que cauſaua medo, todauia eſpreitando,

lines.note: The Portuguese likewise says that, although the thing caused fear, the person nevertheless peeped. Its incomplete clause continues below.
Adds 'and seeing' to the preceding peeping action and leaves the example open with etcetera. This is the final line of the first nozoki entry.
A second nozoki entry means removing or setting aside, not peeping. The identical printed principal parts are retained as a distinct headword with a different gloss.

Nubi denotes male or female servants, paraphrased by the repeated yatçuco. The enlarged N omitted by OCR is restored with its two-line span; the following printed capital V is preserved rather than changed to lowercase u.
Completes moça de serviço, a female servant, paired with the preceding male servant. The row sits beside the enlarged N and remains separate physical text.
Nubibokujuu is assigned the same servant sense as nubi. The final caron-marked u is visible and retained.
Nuboku is paraphrased by yatsuko and shimobe, again servants. The abraded second letter is read as u, consistent with its surviving strokes and the neighboring servant entries, rather than OCR a.
Nuka is glossed as the husk of bate, corresponding to grain husk or bran. The historical Portuguese crop word is retained without replacing the source gloss with a modern technical label.
This separate nuca, alternatively nucadori, is a bird name. The gloss gives no species description; its distinction from the preceding grain-husk entry is preserved.

runs.text: Fruito que ſe dà antre as folhas dos

lines.note: Nukago denotes the small growth borne among the leaves of wild yams. The source calls it a fruit; that wording and the historical headword are preserved rather than modernized to mukago or a botanical classification.
Identifies the plant as wild-growing yams, completing the preceding fruit description. This short row belongs to nukago.
Nukamiso is explained as miso made from rice bran. Miſo occurs inside the Portuguese definition and qualifies as an embedded Japanese typeface term, unlike the headword itself.
Nukari denotes being careless or insufficiently alert. The divided a- begins avisado on the next row, where failure to act promptly is added.

runs.text: uiſado, ou tardar em dizer, ou fazer as cou-

lines.note: Completes avisado and describes delay in saying or doing things. The final cou- begins cousas and retains its visible line-end division.
Completes cousas a tempo, doing or saying things in time. The scan reads ſas a tempo rather than OCR ſara iempo; both word boundaries are visible.
Nukarimono or nukattamono is a careless person, continuing the preceding column's vocabulary of negligence. The Portuguese Homẽ preserves its nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: cuidado, ou pouco auiſado, & que deixou de di

lines.note: Completes descuidado and describes someone insufficiently alert who failed to speak at the proper time. The line ends with di without a printed hyphen; dizer continues below.

runs.text: zer, ou falar as couſas a ſeu tempo.

lines.note: Completes dizer and restates speaking at the right time. The closely related verbs dizer and falar are both retained as printed.

This nukari means being pierced through, unlike the preceding negligence sense. The narrow, weak vowel after p is retained as i in traſpißado; context suggests traspassado, but enlargement does not securely justify replacing the printed-looking i with a.
Gives sword or spear as the piercing instrument and illustrates yari ni nukatta, being pierced by a spear. The nasal abbreviation cõ is retained.

runs.text: Meteoſe a lança pollo corpo. X.

lines.note: The spear passed into or through the body. The scan reads Meteoſe with t, not OCR Meleoſe; the final upright X. is the regional usage label.
Nukashi means saying something, here explicitly contemptuous speech. The aita principal part reflects the historical s-verb pattern; the Portuguese deſ- begins desprezo below.

runs.text: prezo com q̃ ſe reprehende dizendo que falais?

lines.note: Completes desprezo and explains its use in a rebuke, 'what are you saying?' The abbreviated q̃ remains unexpanded in the transcription.
Nani wo nukasuka illustrates the contemptuous question 'what are you saying?' The Portuguese dize- continues below; the question mark after the Japanese is visible.
Completes dizeis and adds the upright B. low-register label. The label qualifies the derogatory expression rather than belonging to its italic translation.
Nukaebi names a kind of shrimp. The source supplies no further species identification; the tilde is retained over e in camaroẽs.
Nukui means warm or being warm. The scan has u after N, not OCR a; the following adverb and noun forms reinforce the same stem.
Nukuu is the long-u adverbial form accompanying nukui. It occupies its own indented physical line and retains its caron.
Nukusa is the corresponding -sa noun, warmth. It is a separate printed derivative row, not a missing Portuguese definition.
Nukume is the transitive warming verb. The historical Portuguese Aquentar is retained; Item introduces warming eggs by incubation.

runs.text: Chocar o paßaro os ouos. Vt,

lines.note: The additional sense is a bird incubating its eggs. Tori tamago begins the Japanese example; its object particle is printed on the following line.
Completes tori tamago wo nukumuru, the bird warming or incubating its eggs. The object particle begins this physical row and is not reattached across the line in the transcription.

Nukumedori is introduced as a small bird used for warmth by eagles or hawks in the dictionary's account. Agueas is the printed Portuguese form; the note reports the historical definition rather than verifying the described animal behavior.

runs.text: falcoẽs apertão antre as vnhas pera ſe aquenta-

lines.note: Continues the historical account: hawks hold the little bird in their talons to warm themselves. The tilde is over e in this falcoẽs, unlike falcões at the page opening.
Completes aquentarem and specifies cold weather as the setting. This closes the dictionary's explanation of nukumedori.
Nukumori is the intransitive warming verb, glossed as becoming warm. It contrasts with the transitive nukume above.
Nugi means taking off clothing or equipment. Haramaki wo begins an example concerning removal of armor, completed by nugu below.
Completes haramaki wo nugu, taking off armor. Katana wo nu- begins an example about drawing a sword, for which the dictionary subsequently prefers a different verb.
Completes nugu but marks nuku as the preferable verb with Latin potiùs. The Portuguese explains unsheathing the katana, whose name is divided Ca/tana without a visible terminal hyphen.
Tana completes the embedded sword-name Catana from the previous row. Tabi wo nugu then illustrates taking off tabi; the Portuguese object is continued below.
Tabis completes the Portuguese translation of removing tabi footwear. The Japanese loan appears inside that explanation with a Portuguese plural ending and is not a standalone Japanese example.

runs.text: O deſpir a manga atè a cinta. Vt,

lines.note: Nugikake names taking a sleeve off down to the waist. The grave in atè and the printed wording are preserved without substituting a modern clothing term.
Nugikake wo suru is the Japanese example of performing that partial undressing. This complete Japanese example is not an embedded Portuguese typeface term.
The verb nugikake describes removing the garments downward. Its continuation specifies remaining partly undressed, distinguishing it from completely taking clothes off.

runs.text: botalos em baixo, ficãdo meo deſpido.

lines.note: The garments are lowered while the person remains half dressed. Ficãdo retains its nasal abbreviation and meo its historical vowel spelling.
A separate nugikake entry applies the verb to drawing a sword slightly. The Portuguese pou- begins pouco on the next row.
Completes drawing the katana a little. Catana has a visible t, not OCR i; X. marks the regional usage, and Meliùs introduces the preferred form nuqicaquru across the line break.
Completes Nuqi-caquru, the preferred sword-drawing form. The initial c on this continuation is visibly lowercase, not the OCR's capital C.
Nugikae means changing garments, with equipment added below. The printed ye in the headword is retained rather than replaced with modern kae spelling.
Adds arms or armor to the things changed. This short continuation completes nugikae before the separate discarding verb.
Nugisute denotes stripping off and discarding garments or equipment. The historical tsuru principal part is retained as printed.
Completes the discarded clothing and armor, then introduces removing footwear. The terminal division mark in Deſ- is clear and belongs to Deſcalçandoſe on the following row.
Completes Descalçandoſe and specifies throwing off the footwear after taking it off. It is the second sense of nugisute.
Nugioki means taking garments or armor off and setting or leaving them down. The damaged vowel after N is read as u, agreeing with the visible nugi- sequence, rather than OCR a.
Completes deixar and names clothes or armor as what is left after removal. The physical break remains dei-xar rather than being joined editorially.
Nui is the stem of nuu, sewing with a needle, followed by its long-u principal parts. The initial sequence is read as nui, not as the nasal-plus-wi suggested by the fallible generated hint.

runs.text: Dobra, ou bainha que ſe faz no veſ-

lines.note: Nuiage is a fold or hem sewn into a garment. The word veſ- continues below, where the reason for making the fold is given.
The garment is too long, so the fold shortens it. Nuiage suru is the Japanese example for making that sewn adjustment.
The verb nuiage describes raising or taking up a garment by sewing. Aleuãtar preserves the nasal abbreviation rather than expanding it to levantar.

runs.text: tido fazendo lhe algũa dobra, ou refego.

lines.note: Completes vestido and explains making a fold or tuck in it. Refego is retained as the source's tailoring word.
Nuiawase means joining things by sewing. The scan reads Coſendo, with final o rather than OCR a, matching the gerund construction.
Completes the sewing definition as attaching one thing to another. This is the final body row; the signature and catchword below are separate furniture.
The catchword anticipates Nuicucumi at the opening of f374. It is separated from the signature rather than left in one OCR furniture string.
